beats.headline: Stop copy-pasting boilerplate across 40 services.
beats.subline: Build versioned starters instead. Here is the industry-standard two-module layout.
beats.narration: Copying filters and security configs into forty services creates massive drift. You need a custom starter. But don't just dump code into one JAR—split it into two modules to keep your dependency graph clean.

beats.title: The Two-Module Split
beats.subtitle: Decoupling logic from dependencies

nodes.label: Starter Module
nodes.detail: Empty aggregator JAR; defines transitive dependencies only.

nodes.label: Autoconfigure Module
nodes.detail: Contains the actual Java code, beans, and imports file.

nodes.label: Consumer App
nodes.detail: Depends on the Starter; gets defaults automatically.

beats.narration: The starter module is just an empty aggregator that pulls in dependencies. The autoconfigure module holds the actual logic. This lets advanced users swap out transitive dependencies without breaking your entire library.

beats.title: Marking Dependencies as Optional

steps.explanation: Critical! Prevents your starter from forcing web dependencies on non-web services.

beats.narration: Always mark optional dependencies as true. This ensures your library doesn't pollute the classpath of services that don't need those specific features, like web or validation.

beats.title: Registration: Then vs. Now
beats.narration: Forget spring dot factories. In Boot 3, use the imports file. It's a simple text file that loads faster and plays nice with GraalVM native images.

beats.title: Part 1 Summary
takeaways: Split into Starter and Autoconfigure modules
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Mastering @Conditional annotations to make your starter bulletproof →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we tackle conditional logic so your starter only activates when it's actually needed.

beats.headline: Your starter is crashing other teams' apps.
beats.subline: Use @Conditional annotations to stay out of the way when prerequisites are missing.
beats.narration: A good starter stays invisible until it's needed. If you don't use the right conditional annotations, your beans will conflict with user code or crash on missing dependencies.

beats.title: The Conditional Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Evaluation order matters

nodes.label: 1. @ConditionalOnClass
nodes.detail: Check if required types exist on classpath.

nodes.label: 2. @ConditionalOnProperty
nodes.detail: Check if the feature is enabled in YAML.

nodes.label: 3. @ConditionalOnMissingBean
nodes.detail: Let the user override your default bean.

beats.narration: Spring evaluates these in order. Check for classes first, then properties, and finally, use MissingBean so users can easily override your defaults with their own implementations.

beats.title: Safe Class Checking

steps.explanation: Spring uses ASM to read bytecode. No ClassNotFound errors at runtime!

beats.narration: Don't worry about ClassNotFound errors. Spring uses ASM to inspect bytecode metadata. It evaluates to false cleanly if the class is missing from the consumer's classpath.

beats.title: The User Override Pattern

steps.explanation: If the user defines their own MyService, this bean is skipped automatically.

beats.narration: This is the secret sauce. By using ConditionalOnMissingBean, you provide a sensible default that automatically steps aside the moment a developer defines their own version.

beats.title: Part 2 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Type-safe configuration with Records and Validation →
beats.narration: Conditionals make your starter robust. In Part 3, we look at ConfigurationProperties and how to fail fast if a user provides bad config.

beats.headline: Stop reading properties as raw strings.
beats.subline: Use @ConfigurationProperties with Java Records for instant validation and type safety.
beats.narration: Hardcoding @Value strings is a maintenance nightmare. In Boot 3, we use Java Records bound to configuration properties. It's immutable, type-safe, and validates at startup.

beats.title: Immutable Configuration Records

steps.explanation: Triggers Jakarta Bean Validation on startup.
Fails fast if config is missing or invalid.

beats.narration: Using a record makes your config immutable. Add @Validated, and Spring will abort the application startup if a user provides a negative threshold or an empty header name.

beats.title: IDE Autocomplete
beats.caption: Generate meta-data for developers
beats.narration: Don't forget the configuration processor. It generates a JSON file that gives developers autocomplete and Javadoc right inside their application dot YAML files.

beats.title: Startup Experience
beats.narration: You want your app to fail during boot, not during a live request. ConfigurationProperties forces the error early, saving you from debugging production incidents.

beats.title: Part 3 Summary
takeaways: Use Java Records for immutable config
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Testing your starter with ApplicationContextRunner →
beats.narration: That's how you build safe config. In Part 4, we wrap up by testing your entire starter in milliseconds using ContextRunners.

beats.headline: Stop smoke-testing your starter manually.
beats.subline: Use ApplicationContextRunner to verify every conditional branch in milliseconds.
beats.narration: Stop creating demo apps to test your library. Spring Boot provides ContextRunners that build a mini-context in memory, letting you verify your starter's behavior in milliseconds.

beats.title: Testing Conditional Logic

steps.explanation: Creates a real, lightweight Spring context.

beats.narration: The runner lets you simulate any environment. You can toggle properties, filter the classpath, or provide custom user beans to ensure your starter behaves exactly as expected.

beats.title: Debugging Conditions
beats.caption: Why did my bean not register?
beats.narration: If things go wrong, run with --debug. Spring will print a full conditions report, showing you exactly which condition matched and which one blocked your bean from registering.

beats.title: Starter Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: From build to deployment
beats.narration: You've mastered the lifecycle: compile-time metadata, boot-time evaluation, and runtime injection. Your starters are now production-grade, versioned, and fully testable.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Build for the platform, not just the app
